utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Chester Stamp, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to greet all those present, representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the staff of this courtroom, bearing especially in mind the interpreters. We are resuming our hearings after several days' break, prior to which we had three months of continuous hearings of witnesses. So after a few days' break, we are resuming our work today. I have been informed of a problem linked to the communication of documents. And due to this, the witness planned for today cannot be usefully heard. The Defence has been informed, and they have conveyed their inability to proceed with the cross-examination. We have been provided with a written motion. The the Prosecution has also responded in writing, telling us that the request of the Defence meets with no objection on their part. Under those conditions, the witness planned will not be heard today. His testimony will be postponed to a later date. The Chamber takes note of this problem, of course, and by an oral ruling we grant the request, as well as the remarks made by the Prosecution, who will delay the hearing of the witness to a later date. I would like to know whether the problems raised in the motion are still outstanding or are they about to be resolved. Mr. Withopf, could you inform the Chamber about the difficulties encountered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, first I refer to the filings you already mentioned in which the situation has been explained to some extent. The situation is as follows: Defence has been made available the more than 2.200 documents stemming from ECMM last Thursday afternoon, and Defence have been informed last Thursday afternoon that the documents are available on the EDS, what's the electronic disclosure system. The EDS is an Internet-based electronic disclosure system for digital material. Using the EDS, the material can be securely searched, reviewed, downloaded, and if necessary it can also be printed. There are a number, a pretty high number of advantages in using the EDS instead of providing Defence with CDs containing such materials, and the advantages are as follows: EDS provides a greatly improved search efficiency; the materials can be searched at once. If you get CDs, you can obviously only search one CD after the other. Using the EDS, it's simpler to track down what materials have been provided. There's no data storage requirement for the Defence. The materials in using EDS are available from any Internet-capable machine from everywhere in the world. And most importantly, EDS is about 60 per cent faster than any other search tool. That means providing the materials in using EDS gave the Defence the opportunity to search the materials as quick as possible, and it was certainly provided early on, in comparison to the Prosecution printing out about 10.000 or so pages of documents and to get it burned on CDs would have taken at the very least the same time as loading the materials into the EDS. That means the materials are available to Defence since last Thursday afternoon. They can search the materials since last Thursday afternoon. The Prosecution understands that the today's witness had to be cancelled but the Prosecution is of the view that all other witnesses scheduled for the next two weeks should be heard as they are scheduled. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I turn now to Defence counsel for them to inform us of problems, if any. According to my understanding, via the Internet it is possible to gain access to the memory of the EDS system and through a code of access which the Defence must have, the Defence can automatically have access to those documents. And thanks to the search engine, by resorting to the EDS system the Defence may have a list of all the documents relating to a particular problem which is in the EDS memory; which means that from any town anywhere, thanks to a computer or a telephone, one can gain access to those documents and they can even be printed out if one has a portable printer. So this allows the Defence counsel to work under the best conditions, noting also that the search engine is very powerful and is 60 per cent speedier than the CD-ROM system. But as the Defence was informed about all this last Thursday, it was impossible for them to prepare for today's witness. So I turn to the Defence to hear their observations, if any. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. President. In response to the matters raised by the Chamber regarding the disclosure of documents coming from the ECMM, the Defence would like to convey the following explanations: First of all, Mr. President, the technical advantages of the EDS system that was put in place almost six months ago are fully acknowledged by the Defence. It is a system which in the medium term will certainly be effective and will allow the Defence team to work more efficiently. Having said that, however, Mr. President, there's a problem of training in the use of this system. When the system was put in place some six months ago - I don't have the exact date - it was accompanied by a directive coming from the Tribunal regarding the use of this system. Regarding the accused that I represent and for the accused Kubura, we never use that system because when it was put in place, the disclosure of documents was virtually completed and so the Prosecution did not resort to this system earlier on in the disclosure of documents. Therefore, one must have a code which we have to obtain here in The Hague which cannot be obtained by telephone, fax or Internet. I obtained this code or password the moment I was informed by the Prosecution that the EDS system would be used, and I obtained this tool on Thursday, the 8th of April, that is, the access code. And we immediately contacted informatics experts, people who know much more than I do, and my knowledge is already more advanced than some other people in the Defence team, and these technicians immediately drew attention to certain problems in the use of this system. So we engaged a person that we remunerated for this purpose to help us in the use of this system more effectively and more efficiently. With our legal assistants and this person that we have hired for this purpose and with the aid of the Tribunal, we have achieved excellent cooperation and identified several problems regarding the use of this system, problems that were resolved last week, that is on Thursday and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Friday. However, from the standpoint of training personally, I am still not capable of using this system, but it has to be someone else within the Defence team. Having said that, Mr. President, all the documents were put on this system, the EDS system, at the end of the day Thursday. We immediately tried to identify documents to burn them on a CD-ROM to be able to use them, and to print them. This effort was completed Sunday afternoon, that is, at the end of the afternoon yesterday; two people worked full time from Thursday afternoon until Sunday afternoon. Therefore, we are in possession of those documents only since yesterday evening. There are more than 2.000 documents consisting of more than 8.000 pages. I have already discussed the situation with my colleague from the Prosecution, and he told me, "Why did you print those documents? You could just search the system for them." There are two reasons for this, Mr. President, the first being the question of training. But a more important question is that an Internet system is not available to the accused, who insist on seeing those documents. Therefore, we have to print those documents. Furthermore, all these documents are in English, and even to show them the most important ones it takes a lot of time to go to the Detention Centre with an interpreter and to go through those documents with the accused. That is why, Mr. President, despite our full and positive appreciation -- actually, we feel it's exaggerated to say that two days was sufficient for us to acquaint ourselves with the document -- we have to tell you today that we need a little more time - not much, but more - to be ready to conduct the cross-examination of some witnesses. In this connection, I would like to underline that my learned friend from the Prosecution has really made a great effort when he communicated to us the timetable for the witnesses for the next two weeks, and my learned friend also identified some documents that may be used by the Prosecution during the examination-in-chief. This certainly facilitates our work, Mr. President, and we are very grateful for this effort made by the Prosecution. Nonetheless, when preparing the cross-examination, Mr. President, it's not simply to challenge the documents produced by the Prosecution, but to find within those 8 to 10 thousand pages documents that might be used to properly represent and defend the interests of the two accused before you at this trial. So it's much more than simply responding to these documents that may be used by the Prosecution. Having said all that, we are able to inform you regarding the schedule proposed by the Prosecution. The witness planned for Tuesday, the 20th of April - I won't mention the name, because we are not in private session - but the witness planned for Tuesday is a local witness, and therefore there's absolutely no problem in proceeding with that witness. The witness planned for Wednesday, the 21st of April is a witness coming from the UNPROFOR mission, and again with him -- with regard to that witness, there's no problem. I go on to Monday, the 26th of April. The witness planned for that date is also a witness from the UN Protection Force, and we have no difficulties in proceeding with that witness. However, Mr. President, for the three other witnesses planned for Thursday, the 22nd of April, Friday, the 23rd of April, and Thursday, the 23rd of April [as interpreted], we could cross-examine those witnesses the following week. And so as not to waste any time, we suggest that we take the dates planned for a discussion on the admissibility of documents and to have that discussion this week. That would be the simplest solution. But I understand that that could cause problems for my learned friend regarding the dates planned for these witnesses. We have two other solutions: The witness planned for Monday who is living in Great Britain, perhaps we could have him heard this week. In brief, we can proceed with the two witnesses, that is, the witnesses for Thursday and Friday. We could do the same as we did for Sir Martin Garrod, that is, have the examination-in-chief and then delay the cross-examination. It is not the best solution. It may be the least useful one for the Chamber and the Defence, but we are ready for every compromise, the requirement being to have some additional time to be able to review those 8 to 10 thousand pages of documents to be ready for the cross-examination. In closing, Mr. President, I have to say in connection with the Monitoring Mission documents, that as you know, Mr. President, this is a situation that dates back to years. On multiple occasions we tried to have those documents being disclosed to the Defence earlier on. However, we are facing a difficult situation. We understand that there are many reasons for this. But because those documents were given to us at the last moment, we cannot jeopardise the rights of the accused. We have to have enough time to fully grasp the gist of those documents. Also, the witness planned for Friday of this week - the name of that witness I think we can mention it, as he is not a protected witness - it is Torbjorn Junhov. Regarding this witness, the witness has a statement that has been disclosed to us from the 10th of October, 1997, and in that statement the witness mentions 35 documents which were given to the Prosecution when giving that statement. In a letter we requested the disclosure of those documents pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii). We didn't receive those documents by January 2004, and we once again sent this list to the Prosecution. But this time it wasn't in a letter but simply by hand. And then in April, that is, on the 7th of April, we underlined once again to the Prosecution that we still hadn't received the 35 documents that were mentioned in the statement of this witness. To this day we still haven't received those documents. Yesterday evening, having in our possession the ECMM documents, we tried to find those 35 documents because some of them belonged to that collection and we did a search on the EDS system and we found five documents out of the 35. For the others, they are not ECMM documents, but we still do not have them in our possession. On the 15th of April, we received documents that may be used during the examination-in-chief of this witness by the Prosecution. Among those documents there are two that are on the list for the witness Junhov. Those two documents are not in our possession and we were unable to find them among the 2.200-something ECMM documents nor among the documents we received from the Sarajevo collection or among the other documents disclosed to us earlier on. For all these reasons, Mr. President, we would request respectfully a rearrangement of the schedule. We do not wish to waste a single day of hearing. We are ready for every compromise, simply to have some additional time to review those documents. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do the other Defence counsel wish to comment? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Mr. Bourgon has indicated, this is a joint application on behalf of both accused. The Defence team for Mr. Kubura is in a similar situation where, as a result of the sheer volume of documents which we have to review, we do need extra time in order to prepare for the cross-examination of these witnesses, not because the Prosecution necessarily will rely on all of those documents but because it is critical to our cross-examination in order to present a full and proper defence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf, the Defence raises two important points. The simplest one has to do with witness Junhov, who mentions 35 documents in his written statement, and the Defence hasn't obtained those documents to this day. They looked for them. They traced some, but a large number are still missing. Therefore, this is a very specific problem, and it would be normal for the Prosecution to be able to provide to the Defence the missing documents before the hearing of that witness. That is the first problem, which seems to me can be easily resolved. The second problem is linked to the cross-examination by the Defence upon reviewing the documents in the EDS system, and in this connection the Defence is suggesting modifications in the order of the witnesses and they have suggested several possibilities: One, which would be supported by the Chamber of course, would be that the hearings for the 27th and 28th planned for the admission of documents could be held this week instead and two witnesses could be postponed to those dates, which would allow the Defence to prepare properly. It is now up to the Prosecution to tell us now, having learnt of the objections of the Defence, what they could do with regard to the problems linked to the access of these documents. I wish to underline - and the Defence is quite right in that respect - that if there are documents which are in English, they need to have to translate them for the accused, that the accused have to convey their opinion in their own language, and all this takes time. That is quite obvious. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let me briefly respond to the lengthy speech of my learned colleague. I myself was given a presentation on the EDS system last Friday. The EDS system is a pretty straightforward situation, and it took me 45 minutes to understand it. That's as simple as it is. In respect to the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, maybe you need 45 minutes, but maybe Defence counsel needs five times more. Maybe they're not as skilled in computer technology as you are. So the Chamber is not here to judge the abilities of either party. You tell us that you were able to resolve the problem in 45 minutes. Perhaps Mr. Bourgon needs five times more. But the Chamber cannot be a judge of the abilities of the two parties regarding the understanding of this system, even though there are -- one side may be more numerous than the other. But never mind. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may refer to Rule 68(B), Mr. President. Rule 68(B) says that disclosure can be done in electronic format, and the disclosure is done on the day the other party has been provided the electronic copies of such documents. So I certainly oppose any suggestion that the materials were only be made available today. They were made available on Thursday last week. The other observations in respect to the scheduling: I understand that the witness for tomorrow shouldn't be a problem. I understand that the witness who is scheduled for Wednesday shouldn't be a problem. The witness who is scheduled for Thursday, I don't understand the Defence request, but the witness who is scheduled for Thursday is not an ECMM witness. This witness is a BritBat witness, and we heard a number of BritBat witnesses without the Defence raising any objections. So I certainly would oppose any suggestion to reschedule the witness who is scheduled for Thursday this week. The witness whose name has already been mentioned - namely, Mr. Torbjorn Junhov - he is quite correctly an ECMM witness. In respect to the documents, I can inform the Trial Chamber that they will certainly be provided in time. The witness who is scheduled for Monday, for today in a week, is again a BritBat witness. And there's only one further ECMM witness next week. Unfortunately - and I have explained this repeatedly - we are talking about witnesses in pretty high positions. It is for a number of obvious reasons not possible to let them come for examination-in-chief and then tell them, "You have to come at whatever later point whenever it's suitable again for the cross-examination." These witnesses are, in their majority, army officers, still-serving army officers, dispersed all over the world. And I'm not only talking about the costs which are involved. It's just pretty difficult to schedule such witnesses on very short notice. The Prosecution, as repeatedly clarified, understands the situation of the Defence, but it wishes to make the Defence and the Chamber aware of the fact that rescheduling such witnesses will end up in a very difficult situation in terms of the schedule as such, since it would basically mess up the schedule for the next two weeks. And it will certainly result in a situation as today, that there won't be witnesses available. Therefore, the Prosecution certainly opposes rescheduling the witness who is scheduled for Thursday this week, and I don't see any problem why the witness who is scheduled for Thursday next week - that means about 10 to 11 days from today - why he shouldn't be heard on Thursday next week and also be cross-examined on Thursday next week. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to Mr. Bourgon in a minute. Regarding the witness for Wednesday, you are telling us that there's no problem. Mr. Bourgon, you heard the remarks by the Prosecution regarding the witness for Thursday and next Monday who are from the British Battalion, and therefore indeed there is no special need to link their testimony with the EDS documents. Regarding the witness for Thursday, the 28th of April, you have more than ten days to prepare for him, so in the opinion of the Prosecution it would be possible to hear this witness on the 29th of April. Regarding witness Junhov, the Prosecution promises to give you the documents. Mr. Bourgon, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very quickly. Regarding Morsink for the 29th of April, there's no problem. That's what I said. All we wanted was for that witness to be next week. So there's no problem hearing Morsink on the 29th of April. Regarding witness Chambers, he is not a BritBat witness, he's a witness of the United Nations mission. He is a native of Great Britain. He's a Briton. But he worked in the central command of the United Nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This witness, Mr. President, he only dealt with documents during his mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had access to all milinfosums. He had access to all the reports of the ECMM, to the reports of each of the contingents. He collected those documents, and he summarised them. Therefore, to prepare ourselves properly for the cross-examination of this witness we believe that we need to consult all the ECMM documents, and that is why his position is different from the position of other witnesses. But we will be ready as of Monday. All we are asking, Mr. President, is a couple of days. Finally, for witness Junhov, this witness was planned for next week anyway, so there shouldn't be any problem, as he was already planned for the following week. Regarding documents, my learned friend tells us that he will provide them, but according to Rule 66(A)(ii) those documents are normally disclosed at the very beginning. 66(A)(ii) says that a statement of a witness who will be called, that statement is disclosed to the Defence but it should be accompanied by all the documents given to the Prosecution. And we have been waiting for those documents for a long time. We don't need to mention the number of months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The advantage of this kind of adversarial system is to be able to grasp fully the problem. Regarding the witness for Thursday and Friday, the Defence tells us that this witness in his mission with the UN had two roles: To synthesise documents from the British Battalion, but also he had to consult the reports of the European Monitors. Therefore, this witness is not, contrary to what the Prosecution tells us, a BritBat witness but someone whose duty was to deal with ECMM documents, which changes the situation. And the Defence is suggesting that we postpone the hearing of that witness to Monday, the 26th, which would allow the Defence to prepare better for the cross-examination. And then the witness for Monday, the 26th could then perhaps be moved to Friday, the 23rd, because as he is from the British Battalion he may be able to do that or not - I don't know - but from now until Friday you have several days to deal with that. Mr. Withopf, regarding the witness Mr. Chambers for the 22nd and 23rd, you have taken note of the fact the Defence appears to link his testimony to the documents of the ECMM and that, therefore, we have a problem on our hands. If you stand by your position for Thursday, the 23rd [as interpreted], a solution could be for the examination-in-chief to take place either on Thursday or on Friday and the cross-examination would take place on Monday, the 26th. That also could be a possibility. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, Your Honours, at this point in time I'm not in a position to inform you whether the witness Chambers, who is a serving army officer, is in a position to stay over the weekend. I will certainly make the respective inquiries. In trying to reschedule the witness Hunter, we may face the very same problem that the witness, for whatever special commitments, is not in a position to come earlier on respective of the fact that the Witnesses and Victims Unit needs five working days in advance to know in the event witnesses have to be rescheduled. The Prosecution will certainly make, as usual, all efforts to accommodate the Defence wishes; however, I simultaneously wish to inform both the Defence and the Trial Chamber that it may not be very likely that these wishes can be accommodated, due to the fact that we are talking about high-level British Army officers who may have other commitments. But again, the Prosecution will make all efforts in order to ensure a smooth running of the proceedings. I also wish to raise the following issue: The Prosecution was given till the 1st of June, 2004 to present its case. We meanwhile had a number of days for which witnesses couldn't be heard for reasons the Prosecution is not responsible for. I only wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber already now to the fact that the Prosecution at some point in time will certainly raise this issue in more in-depth, since based on the today's oral motion it can already been foreseen that a number of additional days cannot be used in the manner the Prosecution wished and intended to use them. This is just an issue I wanted to raise without going into more detail. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, we understand you will see whether it is possible for Mr. Chambers to remain the weekend and whether Mr. Junhov could come the end of the week, Friday. So you will let us know tomorrow, after tomorrow, what the possibilities are, as you have already mentioned. I would also like to inform the Prosecution that tomorrow's witness -- about tomorrow's witness. You have a document where you say that you expect to tender several documents. You have given references, ERN references, but we haven't received the numbers of those documents in comparison -- within the frameworks of your consolidated list. Could you please indicate those documents, the numbers, compared to the consolidated list, because you have not indicated them within the frameworks of that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I'm not in a position right now to indicate the PT or PTW numbers; however, I understand the consolidated exhibit list is available in electronic format. By just entering the exhibit numbers into the list, they can be found within seconds. But I certainly can provide the Trial Chamber with the PT and PTW numbers in addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Well, has the Defence anything to raise at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, any further problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No, not at this point in time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to adjourn for today. It was more or less a status meeting. And I would like to invite you to come to the hearing tomorrow, which is scheduled for 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.03 p.m.,
